newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seed companies battle for corn market share.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seed companies battle for corn market share.

text.p: U.S. seed companies are in the midst of a transition year, showing off a record number of new corn hybrids in a battle for 1998 seed sales.
"This will be a pivotal year," said Dirck Steimel, a spokesman for Pioneer Hi-Bred International Inc, the leading North American seed corn company.
New hybrids -- including those that are genetically engineered to fight off insects or withstand the use of certain herbicides -- are part of a market share battle being waged in the U.S. Corn Belt.
Pioneer said recently its leading share of the roughly $2.0 billion North American seed corn market declined in 1997 to between 42 and 42.5 percent, a drop of about 1.5 to two points.
DeKalb Genetics Corp, the number two rival, has seen about a half-point rise in its 1997 seed corn market share to about 11.5 percent, analysts estimated.
Both companies this year ramped up their introductions of corn hybrids, a trend that is expected to continue as more genetically engineered products are developed.
Pioneer introduced 27 new corn hybrids this year, while DeKalb sold 23 new hybrids this year, including 12 brought out in late December 1996.

"Most of our customers are willing to try the new stuff," Ed Brummels, a Pioneer sales representative in northeast Nebraska, said. "Whether you're talking about hybrids or equipment, farmers recognize the fact that change is coming and at a more rapid rate."
But farmers may have a hard time choosing between the new seed offerings. Good growing conditions thus far this year could obscure the advantages among seed corn hybrids.
"In ideal growing conditions the difference between good hybrids and poor hybrids isn't that great," Piper Jaffray analyst George Dahlman said.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture has rated 73 percent of the U.S. corn crop in good or excellent condition. But seed companies are quick to point out that a lot can happen to a crop between now and the fall harvest.
For now, smaller outbreaks of European corn borer compared with prior years has made it more difficult to sell corn seed that has been genetically engineered to fight off that insect.
Monsanto Co's insect-resistant YieldGard corn has not had the "market excitement" seen in its other crops, said Robb Fraley, co-president of Monsanto's agricultural sector.

But he said demand was strong for Monsanto's other biotech crops, such as Roundup Ready soybeans, which can withstand the use of Roundup herbicide to kill weeds in the field, and Bollgard cotton, which fights crop-damaging insects.
